note: Paripadal 1.1-13 describes two forms in turn, the white one with the hooded heads, the curved plough and a single earring, then the dark one with the bird banner; Paripadal 15.54-61 lists the single earring, the ringed plough, the tulasi, conch, discus and bird banner in one run of plurals and worships them as the two of great name.
teaches: Song 1 keeps the brothers' marks apart in two portraits, while song 15 pours them into one litany and addresses the pair, so together they show the Balarama and Krishna emblems hardening into a shared catalogue of one double deity.

note: Paripadal 13.22-36 makes the plough-bearer one of three forms of a single god (மூஉரு ஆகிய தலைபிரி ஒருவனை); Paripadal 15 keeps them as two, different in form but one in deed (வேறு வேறு உருவின் ஒரு தொழில் இருவர்), and bows to the two.
teaches: Against song 13's solution, which absorbs the brother as a form of the one god, song 15 keeps two persons and finds their unity in a single deed, like word and meaning, so the Paripadal holds two theologies of the pair.

note: The idyll's rite offers rice mixed with a ram's blood and spreads millet with blood, and calls it worship that brings each seeker what he sought; Tirumular says that in worship the bright flower is not killing other small lives. Read plainly, one counts a killing as part of right worship and the other counts not killing as the best offering.
teaches: Blood offering stands in the oldest Murugan poem as an ordinary part of effective worship, so Tirumular's rule that not killing is the true flower is a reform of an existing Tamil practice, not a restatement of it.

note: Paripadal 12.81-83 has the settled Vaiyai show heaven's beauty as a reflection in its water; Paripadal 16.32-38 makes the flood itself look like the sky through which the star-flowered heavenly Ganga runs, with the lovers' fallen flowers as its stars.
teaches: One poet finds the sky in the clear river after the flood and another in the flood's floating flowers, so the pair shows the Vaiyai as heaven on earth being made both from stillness and from festival litter.

note: The idyll's assembly of gods comes with Brahma 'in mind' and a need it does not name; the Thiruppugazh number-poem tells that Murugan imprisoned Brahma and freed him when the three gods came begging at his feet.
teaches: If the Thiruppugazh's story is the one behind lines 160 to 165, the oldest Murugan poem already assumes the episode of Brahma's imprisonment, and the later hymn only states outright what the idyll leaves as an allusion.

note: The idyll finds the god in every outer place of worship, festival ground, veri ground, grove, river, crossroads and kadamba tree; Sivavakkiyar asks what use any puja is while the Lord being sought is within us. On the reading that the Siddhar rejects outer places and rites altogether, the two are incompatible.
teaches: The idyll widens the god's presence outward to every spot where he is called, and the Siddhar narrows it to the one place inside the worshipper, so the pair marks the two ends of the Tamil argument over where the divine is met.

note: In the idyll the god appears in his own form to a living suppliant and says 'Fear not; I knew of your coming'; in the Thiruppugazh the poet asks that at the moment Death's servants come he appear on the peacock and end his fear.
teaches: The god's appearance and his word against fear, which the idyll promises to any suppliant who makes the journey, the later poet saves for the single hour of death, showing how the guide-poem's promise of a meeting became a plea for rescue.

note: Nakkirar's Eragam is the shrine where brahmins recite the rare six-letter mantra; Arunagirinathar's Eragam is where 'the brahmins of the six letters' (ஆறெழுத்து அந்தணர்) praise his feet.
teaches: The six-letter brahmins of Eragam pass from Nakkirar's description into Arunagirinathar's epithet almost word for word, showing that the later poet read the shrine through this idyll's line 186.

note: Nakkirar gives each of the six faces and the twelve hands a work in the world; Arunagirinathar asks to hold the same faces, arms, feet, vel and peacock in thought every day.
teaches: The list of the god's faces and arms began as a description of what he does for the world and became, in the later hymn, a sequence to meditate on, so the same inventory moved from cosmology to devotional practice.

note: The narrator says the king did not inquire because it was the hour of karma's fruit (தேரான் ஆகி); Kannaki calls him the king who did not inquire (தேரா மன்னா).
teaches: The same failure to inquire is excused by karma in the narrator's voice and charged as guilt in Kannaki's, and she herself also names karma, so the epic holds both causes together rather than choosing one.

note: The idyll says those who worship with offerings of goat's blood and red millet obtain what they ask; Sivavakkiyar says that offering goat and cock at the shrine when you are sick does not stop you wasting away. The claims about whether such offerings work are incompatible.
teaches: The Siddhar's mockery of goat and cock sacrifice is aimed at a rite the Sangam idyll describes in detail and promises results from, so his scepticism attacks a claim with a long and respected Tamil history.

note: Nakkirar calls the god 'bull among poets of praised good speech' (புலவர் ஏறே); the Thiruppugazh says Murugan delighted in the poems of Keeran (Nakkirar) and taught him grammar.
teaches: The idyll's epithet makes the god a poet, and the later tradition turns that into a story in which the idyll's own author becomes the god's pupil, so the poem's praise of the god's speech came back as the poet's legend.

note: Kural 215 likens the wealth of a wise man who helps the world to the village tank filled with water; Paripadal 16.1-4 likens the banks, worn away as the flood carries off pepper, sandal and curd foam, to the giving of a generous lord.
teaches: The Kural uses full water as the image of a giver's wealth, and the Paripadal uses a giver as the image of water taking from its banks, so the pair shows the river-and-giving figure running both ways, with the Paripadal stressing that giving is a wearing away.

note: Nakkirar defines the brahmins of Eragam by their outward order (six duties, three fires, sacred thread, wet cloth, chanting at set hours); Tirumular defines the true brahmins by meditating on the mantra and riding the chariot of love so as not to sink in maya.
teaches: The same figure of the mantra-reciting brahmin is praised by the idyll for keeping the forms and by Tirumular only for the inner love the forms should lead to, which shows the Saiva yogic tradition re-grounding a figure it inherited.

note: Kural 83 says the life of one who tends guests daily does not fall into ruin; the verse says a family gains glory by the food it gives.
teaches: The couplet answers the fear that giving food ruins a house; the verse claims more, that it is the source of the family's distinction, so feeding is shown as both safe and the very thing that ranks a house.

note: Kural 4 says those who reach the feet of the one without liking or aversion have no suffering anywhere at any time; Paripadal 15.49-53 says the god appears in whatever world and removes suffering when people are troubled, and sends worshippers with their families to his hill.
teaches: The Kural puts the movement on the devotee who reaches the feet, while the hymn puts it on a god who comes into each world and on the pilgrim's journey to one hill, so release from suffering is framed as both an inward arrival and a visit.

note: The seeker says it is hard for living beings to know the god to his measure (நின்னளந்து அறிதல் மன்னுயிர்க்கு அருமையின்); Tirumular says Vishnu, Brahma and the gods, measuring with thought, cannot conceive the Lord, who stands beyond all measuring.
teaches: The theme that the god cannot be measured, which Tirumular argues through the gods' failure, is already in the Sangam idyll as the suppliant's reason for coming to the feet, so unknowability led to approach rather than to despair from the start.

note: Paripadal 13.10-13 says the god's chest holds by right (உரிமை) the heaven of those who worship it; Paripadal 15.15-18 says heaven is hard to climb unless the tulasi-wearer grants it, but is gained easily, by right (உரிமை), at Maalirunkunram.
teaches: The same claim of a worshipper's right to heaven is lodged first in the god's body and then in a hill one can walk to, so the pair shows Thirumal's grace being given a place on the map near Madurai.

note: Kural 18 warns that if the sky dries up, festival and worship will cease here, even for the gods; Paripadal 16.48-55 prays that the sky never refuse, so that the sandal, garlands, smoke and offerings of the river festival never dry and the Vaigai never runs dry.
teaches: The Kural states the dependence of worship on rain as a general warning, and the hymn turns the same dependence into a prayer said at the festival it describes, so the couplet's rule is shown at work in the Vaigai rites.

note: In the idyll, dancing on every hill with the hill women is the god's settled nature (குன்றுதொறாடலும் நின்றதன் பண்பே); in the Thiruppugazh, Kunruthoradal is the name of a shrine where the hill tribes worship him with frenzied dance (வெறியாடி).
teaches: A phrase that in the Sangam idyll describes the god's habit among the hill people became by Arunagirinathar's time the proper name of a shrine, so the idyll's description is the origin of a later place of pilgrimage.

note: The sages who have cast out lust and fierce anger walk first into Avinankudi; the Siddhar poet clears lust, anger and the great lie out of his heart so that it can become the Lord's bedchamber.
teaches: Driving out lust and anger is in the idyll the qualification of a class of sages to approach the god's shrine, and in the later poem the housework every devotee must do to make the heart itself the shrine.

note: Paripadal thirattu 12 says those who live in Koodal and Parankunram are the ones truly living, and asks who would go to the world of the gods; Paripadal 15.15-18 keeps heaven as the goal and praises Maalirunkunram as the easy way to it.
teaches: One Madurai poet makes the sacred hill a substitute that makes heaven unwanted and another makes it a means to heaven, so the shrine hills could be praised either as better than the world above or as its gate.
